Update: I've switched to use the `dd` tool to trigger OOM killer. The old method of using the bash variable was making the tests flaky on containerd (confirmed running in a loop). It seems the memory allocation was throttled as the CPU was down to 1% and the allocation was not increasing. The test was hitting the timeout (5min): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1d02d014e8c1f0de84b0b58b2165548182815320/test/e2e/framework/pod/wait.go#L378.

The use of `dd` also makes the test much faster. It is down from about 1min to ~5s.

Also, decreased the requests and memory from 20M to 15M, this still gives some buffer over the minimum required by CRIO, which is 12M. 

Tested that after the change passes all on crio and containerd, both cgrpv1 and cgrpv2 consistency. I've done 40 repeats for each configuration.

I thought that the OOMKiller follows some heuristics, is this test guarantee to kill ONLY the pod under test?
should we tag it as Disruptive if not?

The intention of the test is to induce oom killer by the pod exceeding its limits rather than putting the system low on memory (the pod consumes 20mb which should not put the machine under memory stress), so IIUC the heuristics are not relevent.

However, I'm not sure about that fully and I'm ok with the `Disruptive` label. Maybe it is just safer to add it? What do you think @bobbypage  @haircommander ?
ah, nevermind, scratch my comment, is about cgroups oomkiller,
We likely want to make this [Disruptive] as well.

OOM killer would always kill this specific container as when it exceeds limits. OOM killer may also kill another container when the system is running low on memory, but this theoretically can be triggered by any container, not only this one. WDYT?
it's a single container failure. No disruption for other tests.
+1, this should be an issue since it is a container cgroup OOM, not a OOM at a higher level of cgroup hierarchy.
nit: should we also check the exit code?
Makes sense to assert on the exit code as well, pushed the change
